name: Memory-safety vulnerability identification and exploit construction
identify_givens: A short C program (5-15 lines) with attacker-controlled input (a char* from argv/stdin/file plus possibly an attacker-chosen length), containing a fixed-size stack buffer and/or a heap allocation, and one or more unsafe calls: gets, strcpy, strcat, sprintf, fscanf %s, or memcpy with unchecked length. The problem often states the stack layout (grows down, order of locals, pointer size) or lists primitives (malloc/free/strcat semantics), mentions an existing target function (e.g. do_something) or a flag variable, and later sub-questions name defenses: stack canary, NX/W^X (executable address space protection), ASLR (stack base only vs full), guard pages.
identify_target: Identify the vulnerable lines and say why they are unsafe; construct a concrete attacker input that corrupts an adjacent local (flag/pointer), overwrites the saved return address to reach an existing function, or injects shellcode (stating assumptions about executability and known addresses); then judge for each named defense whether it stops each attack and why, and propose a working countermeasure for the attack that survives.
strategy_name: Trace overflow into layout, then match each defense to the attack it misses

algorithm.detail: Scan for unbounded copies: gets, strcpy, strcat, sprintf, scanf/fscanf %s into a fixed buffer, or memcpy(dst, src, len) with attacker-controlled len larger than the destination size. Also flag uninitialized buffers used with strcat/strlen (out-of-bounds read searching for '\0'), use-after-free (pointer used after free), and type-confusing casts.

Write down the relevant region in address order. Stack (growing down): arguments, saved return address, saved frame pointer, then locals in declaration order (e.g. int result; char input[10];). Note exact byte counts and pointer size (e.g. 4 or 8 bytes). For the heap, note allocation size and adjacent metadata/objects.

Decide what to overwrite: (a) an adjacent local above/below the buffer (e.g. an auth flag result set to nonzero, or a data pointer pwd retargeted so a later strcmp/write compares against attacker bytes); (b) the saved return address, reached with buffer_size + saved_fp bytes of padding followed by the target address; (c) heap metadata or an adjacent object via a heap overflow; (d) a dangling pointer via use-after-free.

Give the payload as a byte count formula. E.g. for char input[10] with result declared before it: 11 bytes with last byte nonzero flips result to 1. For return-address hijack: buffer_size + sizeof(saved_fp) filler bytes, then the address of the existing target function (e.g. do_something), then optional extra words for arguments. For pointer retargeting: filler then the address of the attacker's own buffer.

Assume the corrupted region is executable (state this assumption): place machine code (shellcode) inside the attacker-controlled buffer (stack input or heap tmp), overwrite the saved return address with the buffer's address, and on function return the CPU jumps into the shellcode. State what you assume about knowing the buffer address.

Evaluate each named defense per attack: stack canary (checked just before return) stops return-address overwrites but NOT adjacent-local corruption (flag/pointer hijack happens before the check); NX/W^X stops injected shellcode but NOT return-to-existing-function (ret2libc/do_something); stack-base ASLR hides stack addresses but preserves relative offsets and leaves heap/code addresses known, so a heap-resident payload or code-pointer target survives; full ASLR also randomizes libraries; guard pages between regions trap linear overflows past them but do nothing for overflows within a region or within a single frame.

Replace unsafe calls with bounded APIs (fgets, strncpy, strncat, snprintf, or explicit length check len <= sizeof(dst)), initialize buffers before use, add a canary for return-address protection, and prefer a memory-safe language. State which original attack each fix kills.

variations.name: Adjacent local overwrite instead of return address
variations.detail: dasak18 Part II P3 asks for an input (other than the password) that makes the program run do_something; the shortest answer overflows char input[10] by one nonzero byte into int result, setting auth=1 — no return address needed. Trap: students only write the classic return-address smash and miss the shorter local-overwrite attack; also note pwd is a pointer, so 10+4+4 bytes can retarget pwd to point at input itself, making strcmp(input, input)==0 true. Canaries do NOT stop either of these because the hijack happens before the canary check at return.

variations.name: Heap overflow + uninitialized buffer + strcat
variations.detail: The 2025 reexam P6 mixes a heap overflow (memcpy(tmp, input, len) with len>32) with a stack overflow and an out-of-bounds read (strcat on uninitialized buffer[32]). The algorithm adapts by analyzing each line separately: Line A corrupts the heap, Line C corrupts the stack frame and may also read out of bounds. Trap: forgetting that uninitialized buffer has no '\0', so strcat scans out of bounds before even copying.

variations.name: Defense-quiz with role reversal (stack ASLR vs heap payload)
variations.detail: Questions ask per-defense verdicts: randomizing only the stack base defeats a stack-resident shellcode jump but NOT the same payload placed in heap tmp whose address is known (stack randomization does not move the heap) — a unit/scope trap. Guard pages do not stop an intra-frame stack overflow (attack 6b) but can detect the heap overflow past tmp if placed between heap regions. Adapt step 6 by checking for each defense which memory region it actually protects.

variations.name: Shellcode vs ret2existing-function
variations.detail: Some sittings provide an existing function (do_something) so no injection is needed (jump to its known address); others (6c) demand injected new code, which requires stating the executable-stack assumption and a known buffer address. Notation trap: pointer size is given (4 vs 8 bytes) and changes the padding length in the payload; byte order (little endian) matters when writing the address into the input.

example_problem: The following program is not memory safe (input and len are attacker-controlled): void process(char *input, size_t len) { char buffer[32]; char *tmp = malloc(32); if (tmp == NULL) return; memcpy(tmp, input, len); /* Line A */ free(tmp); /* Line B */ strcat(buffer, input); /* Line C */ printf("%s\n", buffer); /* Line D */ return; }. (a) Identify the lines that have a problem and explain why they are not secure. (b) Explain how an attacker can exploit the vulnerabilities to gain control of execution: which memory region is corrupted, what state is overwritten, how execution is redirected. (c) Explain how the attacker can inject and execute new code, stating assumptions about the binary and memory layout. (d) Can randomizing the stack base counter attack (c)? (e) Can guard pages counter attack (b)? (f) Propose a countermeasure for any surviving attack.

example_steps.work: Line A: tmp points to 32 bytes but len is attacker-controlled, so len > 32 gives a heap buffer overflow. Line C has two issues: buffer is uninitialized, so strcat may read out of bounds searching for the first '\0', and strcat performs no bounds checking, so appending attacker-controlled input overflows the 32-byte stack buffer. Lines B and D are fine (free then no reuse; printf only prints).
Stack frame of process (stack grows down): saved return address, saved frame pointer, then locals char buffer[32] and char *tmp.
Target the saved return address via the stack overflow at Line C (most direct path).

Payload: supply input such that strcat(buffer, input) writes beyond the 32-byte buffer — 32 bytes of filler plus 4 (pointer-size) bytes for the saved frame pointer, then the attacker-chosen address. This overwrites the saved return address; when process returns, the CPU jumps to that address (e.g. an existing function in the binary).

Code injection (6c): assume the stack is executable. Put the machine code in input after the part that corrupts the return address, and set the overwritten return address to point to input itself, so returning from process jumps into the injected shellcode.

Stack-base randomization (6d): yes, it counters attack (c) because the attacker no longer knows the address of buffer; however it does not affect the heap, and the payload is also present in tmp, so the attacker can instead point the return address at tmp (assuming the heap address is known) — attack survives via the heap copy. Guard pages (6e): no, they do not counter attack (b) since the overflow is within a single stack frame; they could only help if placed between heap data structures to detect the overflow of tmp.

Fix (6f): a stack canary is the simple fix for the return-address overwrite; the better fix is to initialize buffer, check len <= 32 before memcpy, and bound strcat to write at most 32 bytes (e.g. strncat or explicit length check).
